los.lo: State that the geoid is an irregular shape based on the surface of the oceans influenced only by gravity and centrifugal force.
los.title: The geoid
los.html:
Theory & physics

The geoid is the irregular surface that mean sea level would take if it extended under the continents. It is an equipotential surface of gravity: shaped only by gravity and the centrifugal force of the Earth's rotation. Because mass is unevenly distributed inside the Earth, the geoid has bumps and hollows of up to about ±100 m relative to a smooth ellipsoid. Heights above MSL (elevations, altitudes on charts) are referenced to the geoid; GNSS heights are referenced to the ellipsoid.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • The geoid is irregular; the ellipsoid is the smooth mathematical model. Don't swap them.
  • Forces that shape it: gravity and centrifugal force only (not tides, not wind).
  • GNSS ellipsoid height ≠ MSL altitude: the difference is the geoid undulation.

los.lo: State that a number of different ellipsoids are used to describe the shape of the Earth for mapping but that WGS-84 is the reference ellipsoid required for geographical coordinates.
los.title: Ellipsoids and WGS-84
los.html:
Theory & physics

The Earth is close to an oblate ellipsoid: flattened at the poles, bulging at the equator (polar diameter about 43 km shorter, flattening ≈ 1/298). Many ellipsoids have been used for national mapping, each fitted to its own region. ICAO requires all published aeronautical coordinates to be in WGS-84 (World Geodetic System 1984), the global reference ellipsoid also used by GPS.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Required reference for aeronautical coordinates: WGS-84 (ICAO Annex 15).
  • Mixing coordinates from different datums can shift positions by hundreds of metres: critical for RNAV approaches and database coding.
  • The Earth is oblate: equatorial diameter > polar diameter.

los.lo: State that the circumference of the Earth is approximately 40 000 km or approximately 21 600 NM.
los.title: Size of the Earth
los.html:
Theory & physics

The circumference of the Earth is approximately 40 000 km or 21 600 NM. This follows from the definition of the nautical mile: 360° × 60' = 21 600 minutes of arc, and 1' of latitude ≈ 1 NM. So 1° of latitude = 60 NM anywhere on a meridian.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • 21 600 NM, not 21 600 km. 40 000 km ÷ 21 600 ≈ 1.852 km per NM.
  • Half the circumference (pole to pole via either side, or antipodal distance) = 10 800 NM.
  • Equator to pole = 90 × 60 = 5 400 NM.

los.lo: Describe the rotation of the Earth around its own spin axis and the plane of the ecliptic (including the relationship of the spin axis to the plane of the ecliptic).
los.title: Earth rotation and the ecliptic
los.html:
Theory & physics

The Earth spins on its axis from west to east (anticlockwise seen from above the North Pole), one revolution relative to the Sun in 24 h, so the Sun appears to move 15° of longitude per hour. It orbits the Sun in about 365¼ days in the plane of the ecliptic. The spin axis is tilted 66½° to the plane of the ecliptic (23½° from the perpendicular to it), and keeps the same direction in space throughout the orbit.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Tilt: 23½° to the normal of the ecliptic = 66½° to the plane of the ecliptic. Both numbers appear in questions.
  • Rotation west → east: the Sun rises in the east and moves westward across the sky.
  • The orbit is slightly elliptical: the Earth is closest to the Sun (perihelion) in early January, during the northern winter. Distance is not the cause of seasons.

los.lo: Explain the effect that the inclination of the Earth’s spin axis has on insolation and duration of daylight.
los.title: Seasons, insolation and daylight
los.html:
Theory & physics

Because the axis is tilted, the Sun's declination (the latitude where it is overhead at noon) moves between 23½° N (summer solstice, ≈ 21 June) and 23½° S (winter solstice, ≈ 21 December), crossing the equator at the equinoxes (≈ 20 March, ≈ 23 September). A high Sun gives more energy per square metre (insolation) and longer days. At the equinoxes day and night are ≈ 12 h everywhere. Beyond the polar circles (66½°) there is at least one day of continuous daylight in summer and continuous night in winter.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Equator: day length ≈ 12 h all year; variation of daylight increases with latitude.
  • Tropics (23½°) = furthest the overhead Sun reaches; polar circles (66½°) = limit of the midnight sun.
  • Seasons come from tilt, not from distance to the Sun.

los.lo: State that geodetic latitude and longitude is used to define a position on the WGS-84 ellipsoid.
los.title: Geodetic latitude and longitude on WGS-84
los.html:
Theory & physics

A position is defined by geodetic latitude and longitude on the WGS-84 ellipsoid. Geodetic latitude is the angle between the normal to the ellipsoid at the point and the plane of the equator (not the angle at the Earth's centre, which is geocentric latitude). Longitude is the angle in the equatorial plane between the Greenwich meridian and the meridian of the point.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Geodetic latitude uses the local normal to the ellipsoid; geocentric latitude uses a line to the centre. Charts and GNSS use geodetic.
  • Coordinates are written latitude first: e.g. N40°25.5' W003°41.2'.

los.lo: Define geographic (geodetic) latitude and parallels of latitude.
los.title: Latitude and parallels
los.html:
Theory & physics

Latitude is the angular distance north or south of the equator, 0° to 90° N or S. Parallels of latitude are small circles parallel to the equator joining points of equal latitude; the equator is the only parallel that is a great circle. Parallels get shorter towards the poles: the length of a parallel = equator length × cos latitude.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Parallels (except the equator) are small circles, so flying along a parallel is a rhumb line, not a great circle.
  • At 60° the parallel is half the length of the equator (cos 60° = 0.5).

los.lo: Calculate the difference in latitude between any two given positions.
los.title: Difference of latitude (d.lat)
los.html:
Theory & physics

d.lat is the arc of a meridian between two parallels. Same hemisphere: subtract; opposite hemispheres: add. Name it N or S according to the direction of travel. Example: from 52°30' N to 47°10' N: d.lat = 5°20' S = 320'. From 10° N to 15° S: d.lat = 25° S.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Opposite hemispheres → add the latitudes.
  • d.lat in minutes = distance in NM along a meridian (5°20' = 320 NM).

los.lo: Define geographic (geodetic) longitude and meridians.
los.title: Longitude and meridians
los.html:
Theory & physics

Longitude is the angle east or west of the prime (Greenwich) meridian, 0° to 180° E or W. Meridians are semi-great circles running from pole to pole; a meridian and its anti-meridian (180° away) form a complete great circle. All meridians converge at the poles and are parallel only where they cross the equator.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • A single meridian is a semi great circle; meridian + anti-meridian = great circle.
  • 180° E and 180° W are the same meridian (basis of the date line).

los.lo: Calculate the difference in longitude between any two given positions.
los.title: Difference of longitude (d.long)
los.html:
Theory & physics

d.long is the smaller angle at the pole between two meridians. Same hemisphere (both E or both W): subtract; opposite hemispheres: add, and if the sum exceeds 180°, subtract it from 360° and reverse the direction. Example: 170° E to 160° W: 170 + 160 = 330° → d.long = 30° E (across the date line).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Sum > 180° → use 360° − sum and change the name (E/W).
  • d.long is not a distance unless multiplied by cos latitude (departure).

los.lo: Define ‘true north’ (TN).
los.title: True north
los.html:
Theory & physics

True north (TN) is the direction along a meridian towards the geographic North Pole. True directions are measured clockwise from TN, 000°–360°. Charts are drawn relative to true north; tracks measured with a protractor on a chart are true unless the chart is a magnetic-oriented product.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Wind in METAR/TAF and on wind charts: true. Wind from ATIS/tower for landing: magnetic.
  • Runways, VOR radials and most en-route tracks in the AIP: magnetic.

los.lo: Measure a true direction on any given aeronautical chart.
los.title: Measuring a true direction on a chart
los.html:
Theory & physics

Measure the angle clockwise from the local meridian at the point of measurement. On a Mercator chart all meridians are parallel so the angle is the same along the line (rhumb line). On a Lambert or polar chart meridians converge, so a straight line crosses each meridian at a different angle: measure at the mid-meridian to get the rhumb-line track (approximately), at the start for the initial great-circle track.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • On a Lambert chart, measuring at the departure meridian gives the initial GC track, not the average.
  • Always align the protractor with a meridian, not with the chart edge.

los.lo: Define ‘magnetic north’ (MN).
los.title: Magnetic north
los.html:
Theory & physics

Magnetic north (MN) is the direction a freely suspended magnet points: along the horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field towards the north magnetic pole (currently in the Arctic Ocean north of Canada, drifting towards Siberia). Magnetic directions are measured clockwise from MN.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • The magnetic poles are not at the geographic poles and they move.
  • Near the magnetic poles the horizontal field is weak and the compass is unreliable (large dip).

los.lo: Define and apply variation.
los.title: Variation
los.html:
Theory & physics

Variation is the angle between true north and magnetic north at a place, named East if MN lies east of TN, West if west. Conversion: True = Magnetic + East variation; True = Magnetic − West variation ("variation east, magnetic least; variation west, magnetic best"). Lines of equal variation are isogonals; the line of zero variation is the agonic line.

Example: TT 090°, variation 5° W → MT = 095°.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • West variation: magnetic is bigger than true. East: magnetic is smaller.
  • Isogonal = equal variation; agonic = zero variation; isoclinal = equal dip; aclinic = zero dip.
  • VOR radials use the variation at the station.

los.lo: Explain changes of variation with time and position.
los.title: Changes of variation
los.html:
Theory & physics

Variation changes with position (shown by isogonals on charts) and with time (secular change as the magnetic poles drift; charts show the year of the data and the annual change, typically a few minutes per year). There are also small daily changes and short-term disturbances during magnetic storms. Runway designators and VOR alignments are periodically updated because of secular change.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Use the variation for the current year: apply annual change × years since the chart's epoch.
  • Magnetic storms (solar activity) can disturb compass readings and HF.

los.lo: Define ‘compass north’ (CN).
los.title: Compass north
los.html:
Theory & physics

Compass north (CN) is the direction the aircraft's compass needle actually points. It differs from magnetic north because of the aircraft's own magnetic fields (ferrous parts, electrical currents). The angle between MN and CN is deviation.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Order of corrections: Compass → Deviation → Magnetic → Variation → True (CDMVT).
  • CN is aircraft- and heading-dependent; MN is not.

los.lo: Apply deviation.
los.title: Deviation
los.html:
Theory & physics

Deviation is the angle between magnetic north and compass north, named East (+) if CN is east of MN, West (−) if west. It changes with aircraft heading and with electrical load, so it is listed on a deviation card produced by a compass swing. Magnetic = Compass + East deviation; Magnetic = Compass − West deviation.

Example: compass heading 270°, deviation +2° (E), variation 4° W → MH 272°, TH 268°.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Deviation depends on heading; variation depends on position.
  • Swing the compass after major modifications, avionics changes, lightning strikes or a change of base to a very different magnetic latitude.

los.lo: Calculate XWC by: trigonometry; and MDR.
los.title: Crosswind component (XWC)
los.html:
Theory & physics

XWC = wind speed × sin (wind angle), where wind angle is the angle between the wind direction and the track (or runway). With MDR (mental dead reckoning) use the clock code: angle as minutes of an hour: 10° ≈ 1/6, 20° ≈ 1/3, 30° ≈ 1/2, 40° ≈ 2/3, 50° ≈ 5/6, 60° and more ≈ full wind.

Example: track 090°, W/V 130/30: angle 40° → XWC ≈ 2/3 × 30 = 20 kt (exact 30 × sin 40° = 19.3 kt) from the left.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Use the same reference for both directions (true wind with true track; magnetic wind with runway).
  • sin 30° = 0.5, sin 45° ≈ 0.7, sin 60° ≈ 0.87: the clock code slightly overestimates around 40–50°.

los.lo: Explain and apply the concepts of drift and WCA.
los.title: Drift and wind correction angle (WCA)
los.html:
Theory & physics

Drift is the angle between the heading and the track made good: the aircraft drifts downwind. Drift is named right (starboard) or left (port). The wind correction angle (WCA) is the angle between the required track and the heading needed to make it good; it is applied into the wind. In steady wind, WCA has the same magnitude as the resulting drift: Track = Heading + right drift (− left drift).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Wind from the left → drift right → heading must be left of track (heading < track).
  • Drift is measured from heading to track; WCA from track to heading.

los.lo: Calculate the actual track with appropriate data of heading and drift.
los.title: Actual track from heading and drift
los.html:
Theory & physics

Track made good = heading + right drift or heading − left drift. Example: heading 075° T, drift 7° left → track 068° T. Use true heading with true track, magnetic with magnetic.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Drift "right" or "+" adds to heading; "left" or "−" subtracts.
  • Do not apply variation to drift: drift is an angle, not a direction.

los.lo: Calculate TKE with appropriate data of WCA and drift.
los.title: Track error (TKE)
los.html:
Theory & physics

Track error (TKE) is the angle between the required track and the track made good, named left or right of the required track. It arises when the WCA flown does not match the actual drift (wrong forecast wind or heading flown inaccurately). Example: required track 100°, heading 094° (WCA 6° left), actual drift 2° right → track made good 096° → TKE 4° left.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • TKE = required track − track made good, named by the side of the aircraft relative to the planned track.
  • TKE compounds with distance: 1° error ≈ 1 NM off track per 60 NM flown.

los.lo: Calculate the heading change at an off-course fix to directly reach the next waypoint using the 1:60 rule.
los.title: Heading correction with the 1:60 rule
los.html:
Theory & physics

The 1:60 rule: 1 NM off track at 60 NM corresponds to 1°. At an off-course fix:

  • Track error (TE) = off-track distance × 60 / distance flown.
  • Closing angle (CA) = off-track distance × 60 / distance to go.
  • Heading change to fly directly to the next waypoint = TE + CA (towards the track).
  • Heading change to regain track in the same distance as already flown = 2 × TE, then turn back by TE on track.

Example: 4 NM right of track after 40 NM, 60 NM to go: TE = 6°, CA = 4°; turn 10° left.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Use distance flown for TE and distance to go for CA. Swapping them is the classic error.
  • Valid for small angles (up to about 20°).

los.lo: Calculate the average drift angle based upon an off-course fix observation.
los.title: Average drift from an off-course fix
los.html:
Theory & physics

If the heading flown is known, the track made good from the departure point to the fix gives the actual drift: drift = track made good − heading. Track made good = required track ± TE (from the 1:60 rule). Example: heading 090°, after 30 NM the fix is 3 NM left of a 090° track: TE = 6° left → TMG 084° → average drift 6° left. To correct, the new heading must allow for this drift as well as the closing angle.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • If you were already applying a WCA, the actual drift = (TMG − heading), not just TE.
  • New heading = required track ± actual drift ± closing angle.

los.lo: State that 1 NM is equal to 1.852 km, which is the average distance of 1' of latitude change on the WGS-84 ellipsoid.
los.title: The nautical mile
los.html:
Theory & physics

1 NM = 1852 m (1.852 km) exactly, the international nautical mile. It equals the average length of 1 minute of latitude on the WGS-84 ellipsoid. Because the ellipsoid is flatter near the poles, 1' of latitude is slightly longer at the poles (≈ 1861 m) than at the equator (≈ 1843 m).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • 1 NM = 1.852 km = 6076 ft (for 1:60 rules use 6000 ft).
  • 1° of latitude ≈ 60 NM anywhere.

los.lo: State that 1' of longitude change at the equator on the WGS-84 ellipsoid is approximately equal to 1 NM.
los.title: One minute of longitude
los.html:
Theory & physics

At the equator, 1' of longitude ≈ 1 NM because the equator is a great circle. Elsewhere, the distance represented by 1' of longitude shrinks with latitude: 1' of d.long = cos latitude NM (departure).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • 1' of longitude at 60° ≈ 0.5 NM; at the poles = 0.
  • Never use d.long minutes as NM away from the equator.

los.lo: Convert between units of distance (nautical mile (NM), kilometre (km), statute mile (SM), feet (ft), inches (in)).
los.title: Unit conversions
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • 1 NM = 1852 m = 6076 ft
  • 1 SM (statute mile) = 1609 m = 5280 ft
  • 1 km = 0.54 NM; 1 NM = 1.15 SM
  • 1 ft = 0.3048 m; 1 m = 3.28 ft
  • 1 in = 2.54 cm; 1 ft = 12 in

Example: 250 km = 250 / 1.852 = 135 NM. 3000 m = 9843 ft.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • km → NM: divide by 1.852 (or × 0.54). NM → SM: × 1.15.
  • Visibility in METAR is in metres, RVR in metres, cloud base in feet: convert carefully.

los.lo: Calculate the distance between positions on the same meridian, on opposite (antipodal) meridians, on the same parallel of latitude, and calculate new latitude/longitude when given distances north-south and east-west.
los.title: Graticule distances and new positions
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Along a meridian: distance (NM) = d.lat in minutes.
  • Across the pole on opposite (antipodal) meridians (d.long = 180°): distance = (90° − lat A) + (90° − lat B) in degrees × 60. This is the great-circle distance.
  • Along a parallel (rhumb line): departure (NM) = d.long (minutes) × cos latitude.
  • New position: d.lat (') = NM north/south; d.long (') = NM east/west ÷ cos lat.

Example: 600 NM east along 60° N: d.long = 600 / 0.5 = 1200' = 20°.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Across the pole is much shorter than along the parallel at high latitude (polar routes).
  • Use the mean latitude if the route changes latitude.

los.lo: Evaluate the effect of wind and altitude on air distance.
los.title: Air distance: effect of wind and altitude
los.html:
Theory & physics

Air distance (NAM, nautical air miles) is the distance flown through the air mass. With a headwind the aircraft must fly more air miles to cover a given ground distance; with a tailwind fewer. At higher altitude TAS is higher for the same IAS, and specific range is usually better, but air distance for a given ground distance still depends only on the ratio TAS/GS.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Headwind → NAM > NM; tailwind → NAM < NM.
  • Fuel and range tables in the AFM are often in NAM: convert to ground distance with the wind.

los.lo: Convert between ground distance (NM) and air distance (NAM) using the formula:  NAM = NM × TAS/GS.
los.title: Converting ground and air distance
los.html:
Theory & physics

NAM = NM × TAS / GS (and NM = NAM × GS / TAS). Time is the same in both frames: t = NM / GS = NAM / TAS.

Example: 500 NM ground, TAS 450 kt, 50 kt headwind (GS 400): NAM = 500 × 450 / 400 = 562.5 NAM.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Check the result: headwind must give the bigger number.
  • Same formula applies to fuel: fuel per NAM × NAM = fuel per NM × NM.

los.lo: Calculate TAS from CAS, and CAS from TAS by: mechanical computer; and rule of thumb (2 per cent per 1 000 ft).
los.title: TAS from CAS
los.html:
Theory & physics

TAS is CAS corrected for density (pressure altitude and temperature). On the mechanical computer (CRP/E6B): set the outside air temperature against pressure altitude in the airspeed window, then read TAS on the outer scale opposite CAS on the inner scale. Rule of thumb: TAS ≈ CAS + 2 % per 1000 ft of altitude (in ISA).

Example: CAS 150 kt at FL 100: 150 × 1.20 = 180 kt.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Higher than ISA temperature → TAS higher than the rule of thumb gives.
  • Above about FL 250 or M 0.5, compressibility matters: use the computer's compressibility correction or Mach number.

los.lo: Calculate TAS from M, and M from TAS.
los.title: TAS from Mach number
los.html:
Theory & physics

TAS = M × LSS, with LSS (local speed of sound) = 38.95 × √T (K) kt, T in kelvin. LSS depends only on temperature. ISA MSL (288 K): LSS ≈ 661 kt. At −56.5 °C (216.5 K): LSS ≈ 573 kt.

Example: M 0.80 at −50 °C: LSS = 38.95 × √223 = 582 kt → TAS = 466 kt.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • LSS falls with temperature, not with pressure.
  • M = TAS / LSS: the same TAS gives a higher Mach number in colder air.

los.lo: Deduce the CAS, TAS and M relationship in climb/descent/cruise (flying at constant CAS or M).
los.title: CAS, TAS and Mach in climb and descent
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Climb at constant CAS: TAS increases (density falls), M increases even faster (temperature and LSS fall).
  • Climb at constant M (below the tropopause): LSS falls with temperature, so TAS decreases; CAS decreases.
  • Constant M above the tropopause (isothermal): TAS constant, CAS decreases.
  • Jets climb at constant CAS then switch to constant M at the crossover altitude; in descent the reverse.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Climbing at constant CAS risks reaching Mmo: hence the change to Mach.
  • Descending at constant M, CAS increases: watch Vmo below crossover.

los.lo: Calculate headwind component (HWC) and tailwind component (TWC) by: trigonometry; and MDR.
los.title: Headwind and tailwind components
los.html:
Theory & physics

HWC/TWC = wind speed × cos (wind angle). With MDR: the component along track = wind × cos angle; quick values cos 30° ≈ 0.9, cos 45° ≈ 0.7, cos 60° = 0.5.

Example: track 360°, W/V 030/40: angle 30° → HWC = 40 × 0.87 ≈ 35 kt; XWC = 20 kt.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Wind angle < 90° from the nose → headwind; > 90° → tailwind.
  • At 60° angle, the headwind is only half the wind; at 90°, zero.

los.lo: Apply HWC and TWC to determine GS from TAS and vice versa.
los.title: GS from TAS with wind components
los.html:
Theory & physics

For small drift angles: GS ≈ TAS − HWC or TAS + TWC. Reverse: TAS ≈ GS + HWC. Example: TAS 240 kt, HWC 35 kt → GS ≈ 205 kt.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • With large crosswinds the GS is a bit lower than TAS − HWC (see effective TAS).
  • GS is used for time and fuel; TAS for air distance.

los.lo: Explain the relationship between GS and TAS with increasing WCA.
los.title: GS and TAS with increasing WCA
los.html:
Theory & physics

When the aircraft crabs into wind, only TAS × cos WCA acts along the track (effective TAS). With a pure crosswind, GS = TAS × cos WCA, which is less than TAS. Large WCAs (slow aircraft, strong wind) reduce GS noticeably: at WCA 20°, cos = 0.94 → 6 % loss.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • A 90° crosswind still reduces GS.
  • Effective TAS matters for slow aircraft; for jets the WCA is usually small.

los.lo: Calculate GS with: mechanical computer (TOV solution); and MDR (given track, TAS and WV).
los.title: Ground speed with the computer and MDR
los.html:
Theory & physics

Computer (TOV solution): set wind direction under the index, mark wind speed up from the centre, set the track, slide TAS under the centre: read drift (WCA) and GS under the wind mark. MDR: XWC with the clock code → WCA = XWC / SF (SF = TAS / 60); along-track component → GS = TAS cos WCA − HWC.

Example: TAS 180 (SF 3), track 090, W/V 060/30: XWC 15 kt → WCA 5° left; HWC 26 kt → GS ≈ 154 kt.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Wind on the computer is plotted from its direction (blowing from), track is where you go.
  • Check sense: heading must point into wind.

los.lo: Perform GS, distance and time calculations.
los.title: GS, distance and time
los.html:
Theory & physics

Distance = GS × time; time = distance / GS; GS = distance / time. Use minutes: time (min) = distance × 60 / GS. Example: 175 NM at GS 210 kt: 175 × 60 / 210 = 50 min.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Convert hours/minutes carefully: 1.4 h = 1 h 24 min.
  • Use the speed factor for mental arithmetic: SF = GS / 60 NM per minute.

los.lo: Calculate revised GS to reach a waypoint at a specific time.
los.title: Revised GS to reach a waypoint on time
los.html:
Theory & physics

Required GS = distance to go / time available. Example: 120 NM to go, required ETA in 25 min → GS = 120 × 60 / 25 = 288 kt. Then TAS = GS ± wind component.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Check whether the required TAS is within the speed envelope and the fuel plan.
  • Common in time-controlled arrival (RTA) problems.

los.lo: Calculate the average GS based on two observed fixes.
los.title: Average GS from two fixes
los.html:
Theory & physics

Average GS = distance between the fixes / time between them. Example: fixes 42 NM apart, 1012 to 1024 UTC (12 min): GS = 42 × 60 / 12 = 210 kt. Use it to revise ETAs and to find the actual wind.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Use the measured distance between fixes, not planned leg distances.
  • Average GS + heading + TAS → actual W/V on the computer.

los.lo: Enter revised navigational en-route data, for the legs concerned, into the flight plan (e.g. updated wind and GS and correspondingly losses or gains in time and fuel consumption).
los.title: Updating the flight log
los.html:
Theory & physics

In flight, record ATA at each waypoint, compute the actual GS and wind, revise ETAs for the following legs, and compare fuel remaining with planned fuel. Time gained or lost × fuel flow = fuel gained or lost. Update the expected landing fuel and check against final reserve plus alternate.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Revised ETA = ATA + leg time at the new GS for each remaining leg.
  • Trend of fuel deviation matters more than a single reading.

los.lo: Estimate average climb/descent gradient (per cent) or glide path degrees according to the following rule of thumb: Gradient in degrees = (vertical distance (ft) / 100) / ground distance (NM)) Gradient in per cent = (vertical distance (ft) / 60) / ground distance (NM)) Gradient in degrees = arctan (altitude difference (ft) / ground distance (ft)). N.B. These rules of thumb approximate 1 NM to 6 000 ft and are based on the 1:60 rule.
los.title: Gradients in degrees and per cent
los.html:
Theory & physics

Using 1 NM ≈ 6000 ft (1:60 rule):

  • Gradient (°) ≈ (height difference (ft) / 100) / distance (NM)
  • Gradient (%) ≈ (height difference (ft) / 60) / distance (NM)
  • Exact: gradient (°) = arctan (height (ft) / distance (ft)).

So 1° ≈ 100 ft per NM and 1 % ≈ 60 ft per NM. A 3° glide path ≈ 300 ft/NM (exactly 318 ft/NM) ≈ 5.2 %.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • 3° ≈ 5 % ≈ 300 ft/NM: memorise this triple.
  • Per cent ≠ degrees: 10 % ≈ 5.7°.

los.lo: Calculate rate of descent (ROD) on a given glide-path angle or gradient using the following rule of thumb formulae: ROD (ft/min) = GP degrees  × GS (NM/min) × 100 ROD (ft/min) = GP per cent × GS (kt)
los.title: Rate of descent on a glide path
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • ROD (ft/min) = glide-path angle (°) × GS (NM/min) × 100
  • ROD (ft/min) = gradient (%) × GS (kt)
  • For 3°: ROD ≈ GS × 5 (= GS × 10 / 2).

Example: GS 140 kt on a 3° ILS: ROD ≈ 700 ft/min.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Tailwind on final → higher GS → higher ROD needed for the same path.
  • Check: 3° at 120 kt ≈ 600 ft/min.

los.lo: Calculate climb/descent gradient (ft/NM, per cent and degrees), GS or vertical speed according to the following formula: Vertical speed (ft/min) = (GS (kt) × gradient (ft/NM)) / 60.
los.title: Vertical speed from gradient and GS
los.html:
Theory & physics

Vertical speed (ft/min) = GS (kt) × gradient (ft/NM) / 60. Rearranged: gradient (ft/NM) = VS × 60 / GS. Example: climb gradient 400 ft/NM at GS 180 kt → VS = 180 × 400 / 60 = 1200 ft/min.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • SID climb gradients are in % or ft/NM over the ground: a tailwind requires a higher rate of climb.
  • 3.3 % (standard PANS-OPS climb) ≈ 200 ft/NM.

los.lo: State that it is necessary to determine the position of the aircraft accurately before commencing descent in order to ensure safe ground clearance.
los.title: Accurate position before descent
los.html:
Theory & physics

A descent must start from an accurately known position, because terrain clearance in the descent depends on where the aircraft actually is. Position errors are greatest after long legs without fixes, or with unreliable navigation aids.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Never start a descent below MSA/MEA on DR alone.
  • Cross-check with two independent sources (e.g. DME and GNSS) before descending in mountainous areas.

los.lo: Draw and correctly label the TOV.
los.title: Drawing the triangle of velocities
los.html:
Theory & physics

The triangle of velocities (TOV) adds two vectors to give a third:

  • Air vector: true heading and TAS (one arrow).
  • Wind vector: wind velocity, drawn downwind (three arrows).
  • Ground vector: track and GS (two arrows), closing the triangle.

Air vector + wind vector = ground vector. The angle between the air vector and the ground vector is the drift. Any two complete vectors define the third.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Arrow convention: 1 arrow heading/TAS, 2 arrows track/GS, 3 arrows wind.
  • The wind arrow points downwind (a wind "from 270" is drawn pointing east).
  • The air and wind vectors run head-to-tail; the ground vector goes from the start of the air vector to the end of the wind vector.

los.lo: Resolve the TOV for: heading and GS (with mechanical computer and MDR); WV (with mechanical computer); and track and GS (with mechanical computer and MDR.
los.title: Solving the triangle of velocities
los.html:
Theory & physics

Three standard problems:

  1. Heading and GS (pre-flight planning): known track, TAS, W/V. Computer: wind down from centre, set track, TAS at centre, read WCA and GS. MDR: WCA = XWC / SF; GS ≈ TAS − HWC.
  2. W/V (in flight): known heading, TAS, track and GS. Computer: set heading at index, TAS at centre, mark the track/GS point, rotate to read wind.
  3. Track and GS (DR): known heading, TAS, W/V. Computer: set heading, wind mark, read drift and GS; track = heading ± drift.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Problem 1 starts from track; problem 3 starts from heading. Mixing them gives a drift error of up to 2 × WCA.
  • Always sanity-check: heading into wind, GS lower with a headwind.

los.lo: Determine a DR position.
los.title: Dead reckoning position
los.html:
Theory & physics

A DR position is calculated from the last known position (fix) using heading, TAS and the forecast or last known W/V over the elapsed time, or simply track and GS. It is the best estimate of position when no fix is available and is used to predict when landmarks or radio aids should appear.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • DR accuracy decays with time: wind errors accumulate.
  • An air position uses heading and TAS only (no wind); a DR position includes wind.

los.lo: Evaluate the difference between a DR and a fix position.
los.title: DR versus fix
los.html:
Theory & physics

A fix is a position determined from external references (visual pinpoint, radio aids, GNSS). Comparing the fix with the DR position shows the error in the assumed wind: the line from DR position to fix, divided by the time since the last fix, is the wind error vector. Use it to correct heading and GS for the rest of the flight.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • The DR-to-fix vector over elapsed time gives the difference between actual and forecast wind.
  • Repeated small errors in the same direction indicate a steady wind error, not pilot error.

los.lo: Define ‘speed factor’ (SF).  Speed divided by 60, used for mental flight-path calculations.
los.title: Speed factor
los.html:
Theory & physics

Speed factor (SF) = speed / 60, the distance covered per minute. TAS 120 kt → SF 2; TAS 180 kt → SF 3; GS 420 kt → SF 7. SF simplifies mental DR: time (min) = distance / SF; WCA = XWC / SF.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Use TAS for WCA; use GS for time and distance.
  • SF 7 → 1 NM every ≈ 8.6 s.

los.lo: Calculate wind correction angle (WCA) using the formula: WCA = XWC (crosswind component)/SF
los.title: WCA from crosswind and speed factor
los.html:
Theory & physics

WCA (°) = XWC (kt) / SF. Derived from the 1:60 rule: sin WCA ≈ WCA/60 for small angles. Example: TAS 150 kt (SF 2.5), XWC 20 kt → WCA = 8°.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Valid for small angles (up to about 15–20°).
  • Max drift = full wind / SF: a 30 kt wind at SF 3 can never give more than 10° drift.

los.lo: Average TAS used for climb problems is calculated at the altitude 2/3 of the cruising altitude.
los.title: Average TAS in the climb
los.html:
Theory & physics

For climb problems use the TAS at 2/3 of the cruising altitude (or 2/3 of the altitude change above the departure level). Rate of climb decreases with height, so the aircraft spends more time in the upper part of the climb.

Example: climb to FL 300 → use TAS at FL 200.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Climb: 2/3; descent: 1/2. Don't swap them.

los.lo: Average TAS used for descent problems is calculated at the altitude 1/2 of the descent altitude.
los.title: Average TAS in the descent
los.html:
Theory & physics

For descent problems use the TAS at 1/2 of the descent altitude, because the rate of descent is roughly constant, so time is spread evenly through the altitude band.

Example: descent from FL 240 to the surface → use TAS at FL 120.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • 1/2 of the altitude band descended, not 1/2 of the cruising altitude, if the descent ends above sea level.

los.lo: WV used for climb problems is the WV at the altitude 2/3 of the cruising altitude.
los.title: Average wind in the climb
los.html:
Theory & physics

The W/V for climb problems is the wind at 2/3 of the cruising altitude (same logic as average TAS).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Interpolate between wind levels on the forecast if 2/3 falls between them.

los.lo: WV used for descent problems is the WV at the altitude 1/2 of the descent altitude.
los.title: Average wind in the descent
los.html:
Theory & physics

The W/V for descent problems is the wind at 1/2 of the descent altitude.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Strong jet-level tailwinds can significantly lengthen the descent distance: plan the top of descent with the wind at the mid-level.

los.lo: Calculate the average climb/descent GS from given TAS at various altitudes, and WV at various altitudes and true track.
los.title: Average GS in climb and descent
los.html:
Theory & physics

Take the average TAS and W/V at the 2/3 (climb) or 1/2 (descent) level, then solve the TOV for the true track to get the average GS. Distance covered = average GS × time in climb or descent.

Example: climb to FL 240, TAS at FL 160 = 300 kt, wind at FL 160 = 40 kt headwind → average GS = 260 kt.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Average GS, not cruise GS, gives the top-of-climb and top-of-descent positions.

topics.title: Ground speed (GS)/distance covered during climb or descent

los.lo: State that most aircraft operating handbooks supply graphical material to calculate climb and descent problems.
los.title: Handbook climb and descent graphs
los.html:
Theory & physics

Most aircraft operating handbooks provide graphs or tables for time, fuel and distance to climb and descend, entered with pressure altitude, temperature, mass and wind. Results are usually in still air; correct the distance for wind using average GS or the chart's wind correction.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Climb data often give values from sea level: subtract the departure-airport values to get the climb from an elevated aerodrome.

los.lo: Calculate the flying time and distance during climb/descent from given average rate of climb/descent and using average GS using the following formulae valid for a 3-degree-glide path: rate of descent = (GS × 10) / 2 rate of descent = speed factor (SF) × glide-path angle × 100
los.title: Time and distance in climb and descent
los.html:
Theory & physics

Time = altitude change / average rate of climb or descent; distance = average GS × time. For a 3° descent: ROD = GS × 10 / 2 = GS × 5 and ROD = SF × 3 × 100. Descent distance on 3° ≈ height (ft) / 300 NM (≈ 3 NM per 1000 ft).

Example: descend 9000 ft at 1500 ft/min = 6 min; GS 240 kt → 24 NM.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • "3 times the height" rule: 30 000 ft → about 90–100 NM descent distance on 3°.
  • Increase the distance for tailwind or for speed reduction.

los.lo: Given distance, speed and present altitude, calculate the rate of climb/descent in order to reach a certain position at a given altitude.
los.title: Required rate to reach an altitude at a point
los.html:
Theory & physics

Required ROC/ROD = height change / time available, where time = distance / GS. Example: 10 000 ft to lose in 40 NM at GS 300 kt: time = 8 min → ROD = 1250 ft/min.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Always use GS (not TAS) to convert distance into time.
  • Allow distance for deceleration before the constraint.

los.lo: Given speed, rate of climb/descent and altitude, calculate the distance required in order to reach a certain position at a given altitude.
los.title: Distance required for a climb or descent
los.html:
Theory & physics

Distance = GS × (height change / rate). Example: GS 270 kt (SF 4.5), descend 12 000 ft at 1500 ft/min → 8 min → 36 NM.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Start the descent earlier with a tailwind (higher GS → more distance).

los.lo: Given speed, distance to go and altitude to climb/descent, calculate the rate of climb/descent.
los.title: Rate of climb or descent from distance, speed and height
los.html:
Theory & physics

Rate = height × GS / (distance × 60) (ft/min, with GS in kt and distance in NM). Example: 6000 ft in 20 NM at 180 kt: 6000 × 180 / (20 × 60) = 900 ft/min.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Equivalent to: gradient (ft/NM) × GS / 60.

los.lo: Recognise which elements would make a ground feature suitable for use for VFR navigation.
los.title: Suitable ground features for VFR navigation
los.html:
Theory & physics

A good feature is unique (cannot be confused with a similar one nearby), large or prominent, contrasts with its surroundings and is shown accurately on the chart. Line features (coastlines, large rivers, motorways, railways) are useful as collecting features; point features (towns with a distinctive shape, lakes, dams, masts, bridges, junctions) give pinpoints.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Combine features: a railway crossing a river near a town is better than a town alone.
  • Small roads and villages change faster than charts are revised.

los.lo: Describe the problems of VFR navigation at lower levels and the causes of reduced visibility.
los.title: VFR navigation at low level and in reduced visibility
los.html:
Theory & physics

At low level the field of view is small, features pass quickly and are seen obliquely, and terrain can hide landmarks. Visibility is reduced by haze, mist, fog, precipitation, low cloud, smoke and sun glare (worst flying towards a low sun). Workload rises (obstacles, airspace, terrain).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • In poor visibility features appear late: plan with large, linear features and stay on DR timing.
  • Sun glare into-sun makes haze look worse: plan legs to avoid flying into a low sun.

los.lo: Describe the problems of VFR navigation at night.
los.title: VFR navigation at night
los.html:
Theory & physics

At night unlit terrain and water are invisible; navigation relies on lit features: towns, major roads with traffic, aerodrome beacons and lighthouses. Coastlines may be visible under moonlight. Town lights can look closer than they are; distances are hard to judge. Cloud and terrain are hard to see, so minimum safe altitude matters even more.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Plan routes along well-lit features and radio aids; know the MSA.
  • Large dark areas (lakes, forests, sea) can be mistaken for cloud and vice versa.

topics.title: Use of visual observations and application to in-flight navigation

los.lo: Describe what is meant by the term ‘map reading’.
los.title: Map reading
los.html:
Theory & physics

Map reading is identifying the aircraft's position by comparing features seen on the ground with features on the chart. Work from map to ground: predict from the DR position and the chart what should appear and when, then confirm it on the ground.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Going ground-to-map (seeing something and searching the map for it) easily leads to false identification.

los.lo: Define the term ‘visual checkpoint’.
los.title: Visual checkpoint
los.html:
Theory & physics

A visual checkpoint is a selected, easily identifiable ground feature along or near the route, used to check position and timing. It is chosen in advance during flight planning and marked on the chart with its planned time.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Checkpoints every 10–15 minutes are typical for VFR.

los.lo: Discuss the general features of a visual checkpoint and give examples.
los.title: Features of a good visual checkpoint
los.html:
Theory & physics

Good checkpoints are unmistakable, visible from a distance and from the planned altitude, and not dependent on season or lighting. Examples: a river junction, a motorway interchange, a large lake, a town with a characteristic shape next to a railway, a prominent mountain peak, a coastline headland.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Avoid single small features (a farm, a minor road).
  • Use a line feature just beyond the checkpoint as a backstop in case you miss it.

los.lo: State that the evaluation of the differences between DR positions and actual position can refine flight performance and navigation.
los.title: Using DR errors to improve navigation
los.html:
Theory & physics

Comparing the DR position with the actual position at each checkpoint shows how the actual wind differs from the forecast. Use the difference to revise heading and GS for the next leg (1:60 corrections) and to update ETAs.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • A consistent drift to one side means the wind is different from forecast: correct heading, not just the position.

los.lo: Establish fixes on navigational charts by plotting visually derived intersecting lines of position.
los.title: Fixing by intersecting position lines
los.html:
Theory & physics

A position line is a line on which the aircraft is known to be at a given time (e.g. a line through a feature in a measured direction, a coastline, a railway). Two or more position lines that cross give a fix. Best accuracy when they cross at about 90°; three lines form a "cocked hat" whose size shows the error.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Position lines crossing at a shallow angle give a poor fix.
  • Transfer an earlier position line along track (running fix) if the lines are not simultaneous.

los.lo: Describe the use of a single observed position line to check flight progress.
los.title: Single position line to check progress
los.html:
Theory & physics

A single position line perpendicular to track (e.g. a railway crossing the route) checks progress (GS and ETA). One parallel to track checks track-keeping. One position line alone does not fix the position.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Perpendicular → timing; parallel → drift.

los.lo: Describe how to prepare and align a map/chart for use in visual navigation.
los.title: Preparing and orienting the map
los.html:
Theory & physics

Before flight: draw tracks, mark distance and time ticks (e.g. every 10 NM or 5 min), headings, checkpoints, MSA, frequencies and airspace. In flight, orient the map so the track points ahead (track-up), fold it so the current leg is visible, and keep the pencil and ruler available.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Track-up orientation makes left/right features on the map match left/right outside.

los.lo: Describe visual-navigation techniques including: use of DR position to locate identifiable landmarks; identification of charted features/landmarks; factors affecting the selection of landmarks; an understanding of seasonal and meteorological effects on the appearance and visibility of landmarks; selection of suitable landmarks; estimation of distance from landmarks from successive bearings; estimation of the distance from a landmark using an approximation of the sighting angle and the flight altitude.
los.title: Visual-navigation techniques
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Use the DR position to know where to look and when.
  • Identify charted features with several characteristics (shape, size, relationship to other features).
  • Choose landmarks considering season and weather: snow hides roads and small lakes; dry seasons shrink rivers; haze hides low features.
  • Distance from successive bearings: when the relative bearing of a landmark doubles (e.g. 45° to 90°), the distance flown equals the distance to the landmark.
  • Distance from sighting angle: distance ≈ height / tan(depression angle); at 45° depression the horizontal distance equals the height; at 1:60, a feature 6° below the horizon from 3000 ft ≈ 5 NM away.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Doubling the angle on the bow: distance run = distance off at the second bearing.
  • Lakes freeze and look like fields; fields flood and look like lakes.

los.lo: Describe the action to be taken if there is no visual checkpoint available at a scheduled turning point.
los.title: No checkpoint at a turning point
los.html:
Theory & physics

If the turning point cannot be identified, turn on ETA (on DR) to the next heading, then check with the next feature (often a line feature as a backstop). Don't orbit searching for the feature: this destroys the DR.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Turn at the ETA, then reassess; use a nearby collecting feature to confirm.

los.lo: Understand the difficulties and limitations that may be encountered in map reading in some geographical areas due to the nature of terrain, lack of distinctive landmarks, or lack of detailed and accurate charted data.
los.title: Map-reading limitations
los.html:
Theory & physics

Map reading is difficult over featureless terrain (deserts, forests, sea, snowfields), over areas with many similar features (many lakes, uniform farmland), and where charts are inaccurate or out of date. Mountains can hide features and produce turbulence. In such areas, rely on DR, timing and radio aids.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Plan more conservative fuel and more frequent radio fixes over featureless areas.

los.lo: State the function of contour lines on a topographical chart.
los.title: Contour lines
los.html:
Theory & physics

Contour lines join points of equal elevation above MSL. Close spacing = steep slope; wide spacing = gentle slope. Closed rings = hills (or depressions if marked). The contour interval is stated in the legend.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Contours give relief shape; spot heights give the highest points.

los.lo: Indicate the role of ‘layer tinting’ (colour gradient) in relation to the depiction of topography on a chart.
los.title: Layer tinting
los.html:
Theory & physics

Layer tinting colours the areas between contours with a graded colour scale (e.g. green for low ground through yellow and brown for high ground) so relief is visible at a glance. The legend gives the height band for each colour.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Layer tints show elevation bands; they do not show obstacles (masts, buildings) above terrain.

los.lo: Using the contours shown on a chart, describe the appearance of a significant feature.
los.title: Reading terrain from contours
los.html:
Theory & physics

From contours you can picture: valleys (contours form Vs pointing upstream, towards higher ground), ridges/spurs (Vs pointing downhill), saddles/passes (between two closed high areas), cliffs (contours merging), plateaus (wide flat area inside a high contour).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • In a valley, V-shaped contours point uphill; on a spur they point downhill.

los.lo: Apply the techniques of DR, map reading, orientation, timing and revision of ETAs and headings.
los.title: Combining DR, map reading and timing
los.html:
Theory & physics

Standard VFR technique: fly the planned heading accurately, note the time at each checkpoint, compare with the plan, correct heading with the 1:60 rule, revise ETAs and fuel. Clock → map → ground: look at the clock, check where you should be on the map, then find it on the ground.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Accurate heading and timing make visual navigation work; map reading confirms it.

los.lo: Explain what needs to be considered in case of diversion, when unsure of position and when lost.
los.title: Diversion, uncertain of position, lost
los.html:
Theory & physics

Diversion: choose the new destination, estimate track and distance by eye or with a ruler, turn onto an approximate heading at once (over a known point if possible), then refine heading, time and fuel; inform ATC.

Uncertain of position: keep flying the heading, check DR, look for a line feature, use radio aids, and consider a circle of uncertainty around the DR position (radius ≈ 10 % of distance since the last fix).

Lost: tell someone early (ATC, distress/urgency frequency 121.5 MHz, PAN), climb if safe for better radio and visual range, conserve fuel, use radar or VDF assistance, and land before fuel or light runs out.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Ask for help early; don't wander looking for features.
  • Never descend below the safe altitude to find your position.

los.lo: Describe the geometric properties of a great circle (including the vertex) and a small circle.
los.title: Great circles, vertex and small circles
los.html:
Theory & physics

A great circle is any circle on the Earth's surface whose plane passes through the centre of the Earth; it divides the Earth into two equal halves. Only one great circle passes through two points (unless they are antipodal, when there are infinitely many). The vertex is the point of highest latitude on a great circle; there the great circle runs exactly east–west (track 090°/270°), and the latitude of the vertex equals the inclination of the great circle to the equator. A small circle is a circle whose plane does not pass through the centre.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Each great circle has two vertices, one in each hemisphere, 180° of longitude apart.
  • Parallels of latitude (other than the equator) are small circles.

los.lo: Explain why a great-circle route is the shortest distance between any two positions on the Earth.
los.title: Why the great circle is the shortest route
los.html:
Theory & physics

On a sphere, the shortest path between two points is the shorter arc of the great circle through them, because the great circle has the largest possible radius (the Earth's radius), so it curves least between the two points. Any other route (rhumb line, small circle) bends more and is longer.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Long-haul flights follow great-circle routes (modified for winds), which look curved on a Mercator chart.

los.lo: Name examples of great circles on the surface of the Earth.
los.title: Examples of great circles
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • The equator.
  • Every meridian with its anti-meridian.
  • Any other circle through the Earth's centre, such as the route London–Los Angeles or the terminator (the day/night boundary).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • The equator is the only parallel that is a great circle.

los.lo: Explain why the track direction of a great-circle route (other than following a meridian or the equator) changes.
los.title: Why great-circle track changes
los.html:
Theory & physics

Meridians converge towards the poles, so a great circle that is not a meridian or the equator crosses successive meridians at different angles: its true track changes continuously along the route. In the northern hemisphere the GC track increases when flying east and decreases when flying west (the opposite in the southern hemisphere). The great circle always lies on the polar side of the rhumb line between the same two points.

The total change of great-circle track between two points equals the Earth convergency between their meridians.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • GC track along a meridian or the equator is constant (no convergency effect).
  • NH, eastbound: the GC route lies north of the rhumb line; initial GC track is smaller than the RL track, final GC track larger.

los.lo: State the formula used to approximate the value of Earth convergence as change of longitude × sine mean latitude.
los.title: Earth convergency formula
los.html:
Theory & physics

Convergency (°) = d.long (°) × sin (mean latitude). It is the angle between two meridians measured along a line joining them, and equals the change of great-circle track between those meridians. At the equator convergency is 0; at the poles it equals d.long.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Use the mean latitude of the two points.
  • In the formula, latitude is in sin; departure uses cos. Don't swap them.

los.lo: Calculate the approximate value of Earth convergence between any two positions, up to 30 degrees difference of longitude.
los.title: Calculating convergency
los.html:
Theory & physics

Example: A 50° N 010° W to B 60° N 020° E. d.long = 30°, mean lat = 55°. Convergency = 30 × sin 55° = 30 × 0.819 ≈ 24.6°. If the initial great-circle track at A is 040° T, the final track at B is 040 + 24.6 ≈ 065° T (NH, eastbound: track increases).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • NH: eastbound GC track increases, westbound GC track decreases. SH: the opposite.
  • Valid as an approximation up to about 30° d.long.

los.lo: Describe the geometric properties of a rhumb line.
los.title: Rhumb line
los.html:
Theory & physics

A rhumb line (loxodrome) cuts every meridian at the same angle: its true track is constant. Meridians and the equator are both rhumb lines and great circles; parallels of latitude are rhumb lines (track 090/270). Any other rhumb line spirals towards the pole without reaching it. On a Mercator chart rhumb lines are straight.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Constant true track = rhumb line, easy to fly with a compass, but longer than the GC.
  • On a Mercator chart a straight line is a rhumb line, not a great circle.

los.lo: State that a rhumb-line route is not the shortest distance between any two positions on the Earth (excluding meridians and equator).
los.title: Rhumb line is not the shortest route
los.html:
Theory & physics

Except along a meridian or the equator, the rhumb line is longer than the great circle between the same two points, because it is not the arc of a circle through the Earth's centre. The rhumb line always lies on the equatorial side of the great circle.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Along meridians and the equator GC and RL coincide; the distance difference is zero.

los.lo: Explain that the variation in distance of the great-circle route and rhumb-line route between any two positions increases with increasing latitude or change in longitude.
los.title: GC versus RL distance
los.html:
Theory & physics

The difference between great-circle and rhumb-line distances increases with latitude and with d.long. Near the equator, or for short routes, the difference is negligible. On long high-latitude east–west routes it is large: e.g. along 60° N for 90° of d.long, the RL is 2700 NM but the GC is only about 2480 NM.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • For an east–west route at high latitude, the GC bulges strongly towards the pole.

los.lo: Calculate and apply the conversion angle.
los.title: Conversion angle
los.html:
Theory & physics

The conversion angle (CA) is the angle between the great circle and the rhumb line joining two points, measured at either point: CA = ½ × convergency = ½ × d.long × sin mean lat. The great circle lies on the polar side, so:

  • NH: GC track = RL track − CA at the start (eastbound), + CA at the end.
  • Radio bearings travel along great circles: to plot a radio bearing on a Mercator chart (rhumb lines straight), convert the GC bearing to a RL bearing by applying the CA (towards the equator).

Example: RL track 080° T, d.long 20°, mean lat 50° N → convergency 15.3°, CA 7.7°. Initial GC track ≈ 072°, final ≈ 088°.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • CA is half the convergency.
  • The rhumb-line track equals the mean of the initial and final GC tracks.
  • On a Lambert chart, straight lines ≈ GC: radio bearings plot directly with the correct (chart) convergency, not the conversion angle.

los.lo: State the requirement for conformality and for a straight line to approximate a great circle.
los.title: ICAO chart requirements
los.html:
Theory & physics

ICAO Annex 4 requires aeronautical charts to be conformal (angles and shapes correct over small areas, scale the same in all directions at a point) and, where practical, for a straight line to approximate a great circle. This is why the Lambert conformal conic projection is the standard for en-route and aeronautical charts at mid-latitudes, and polar stereographic at high latitudes.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Conformality is the most important property for navigation charts (bearings and tracks measured correctly).
  • No flat chart can be conformal and equal-area at the same time.

los.lo: Explain and calculate the constant of the cone (sine of parallel of origin).
los.title: Constant of the cone
los.html:
Theory & physics

On a conical projection, meridians are straight lines converging at the apex of the cone. Chart convergency = d.long × n, where n, the constant of the cone = sin (parallel of origin). The parallel of origin is where the cone touches (or the mid-parallel between the two standard parallels for a secant cone). Polar stereographic: n = 1 (sin 90°); Mercator: n = 0.

Example: parallel of origin 48° → n = 0.743. Between meridians 20° apart, chart convergency = 14.9°.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • n is constant over the whole chart: chart convergency depends on d.long only, not on latitude.
  • n = sin parallel of origin.

los.lo: Explain the relationship between Earth and chart convergence with respect to the ICAO requirement for a straight line to approximate a great circle.
los.title: Earth versus chart convergency
los.html:
Theory & physics

A straight line on a chart represents a great circle exactly only where chart convergency = Earth convergency. On a Lambert chart this is true at the parallel of origin; elsewhere the straight line is a close approximation, slightly different from the GC. Polar stereographic: chart convergency = d.long; Earth convergency = d.long × sin lat → equal only at the pole, close at high latitudes.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • On a Lambert chart a great circle is a curve slightly concave towards the parallel of origin; the straight line is a very close approximation, exact at the parallel of origin.
  • Mercator: chart convergency 0 → straight lines are rhumb lines.

los.lo: Recognise methods of representing scale on aeronautical charts.
los.title: Representing scale
los.html:
Theory & physics

Scale = chart length / Earth distance. Shown as: a representative fraction (e.g. 1:500 000), a graduated scale line, or a statement ("1 cm = 5 km"). On many charts, latitude graduations on the meridians can also be used: 1' of latitude = 1 NM.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • A larger scale (e.g. 1:250 000) shows more detail over a smaller area than 1:1 000 000.
  • Using latitude marks on the side of a Lambert/Mercator chart gives NM directly.

los.lo: Perform scale calculations based on typical en-route chart scales.
los.title: Scale calculations
los.html:
Theory & physics

Earth distance = chart distance × scale denominator. Example: 1:500 000, 12 cm on the chart = 12 × 500 000 cm = 6 000 000 cm = 60 km = 32.4 NM. Reverse: 100 NM at 1:1 000 000 = 185.2 km = 18.5 cm.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Keep units consistent: 1 km = 100 000 cm.
  • Common chart scales: 1:500 000 (VFR), 1:1 000 000 (ICAO world aeronautical chart).

los.lo: Identify azimuthal, cylindrical and conical projections.
los.title: Azimuthal, cylindrical and conical projections
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Azimuthal (plane): the projection surface is a plane touching the Earth, usually at a pole (polar stereographic). Meridians are straight radial lines; parallels are concentric circles.
  • Cylindrical: the surface is a cylinder, usually touching the equator (Mercator). Meridians are parallel straight lines; parallels are straight lines.
  • Conical: a cone touching (or cutting) the Earth along one or two parallels (Lambert). Meridians are straight lines converging to the apex; parallels are arcs of circles.

Exam diagram

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Identify by the look of the graticule: parallel meridians = cylindrical; converging straight meridians with arc parallels = conical; radial meridians with circular parallels = azimuthal.

los.lo: State the properties of a polar stereographic projection.
los.title: Polar stereographic properties
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Projection from the opposite pole onto a plane tangent at the pole.
  • Conformal; meridians are straight lines radiating from the pole; parallels are concentric circles.
  • Chart convergency = d.long (n = 1): correct at the pole, close at high latitudes.
  • Straight line ≈ great circle (very close near the pole).
  • Scale is correct at the pole and expands away from it: at 70° lat it is about 3 % larger; used for latitudes above about 70°.
  • Rhumb lines are curves concave to the pole.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Use: polar navigation, often with a grid overlay (grid navigation) because true direction changes fast near the pole.

los.lo: Calculate straight line track changes on a polar stereographic chart.
los.title: Straight-line track changes on a polar stereographic chart
los.html:
Theory & physics

Because chart convergency = d.long, a straight line's true track changes by exactly the d.long between the two points. Example: straight line from 070° N 020° W with initial track 080° T to a point at 030° E (d.long 50°, eastbound in the NH): final track = 080 + 50 = 130° T.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • On polar stereographic, track change = d.long × 1; on Lambert = d.long × n; on Mercator = 0.

los.lo: State the properties of a direct Mercator projection.
los.title: Direct Mercator properties
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Cylinder tangent at the equator; conformal.
  • Meridians are parallel, equally spaced straight lines; parallels are straight lines, spaced further apart towards the poles.
  • Chart convergency = 0: correct only at the equator.
  • Rhumb lines are straight; great circles are curves concave to the equator (bulging towards the pole).
  • Scale correct at the equator (or at a stated latitude) and expands with sec latitude; the poles cannot be shown.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Straight line on Mercator = rhumb line (constant track), not shortest distance.
  • To plot a radio bearing (a GC) on Mercator, apply the conversion angle.

los.lo: Given the scale at one latitude, calculate the scale at different latitudes.
los.title: Mercator scale at different latitudes
los.html:
Theory & physics

On Mercator, scale ∝ sec latitude (scale is larger, i.e. more expanded, at higher latitudes). With representative fractions: denominator at lat 2 = denominator at lat 1 × cos lat 2 / cos lat 1.

Example: scale 1:1 000 000 at the equator → at 60° N: 1 000 000 × cos 60° / cos 0° = 1:500 000.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Higher latitude → bigger scale → smaller denominator.
  • Use the ratio of cosines; don't subtract.

los.lo: Given a chart length at one latitude, show that it represents a different Earth distance at other latitudes.
los.title: Same chart length, different Earth distance
los.html:
Theory & physics

On Mercator a given chart length represents a shorter Earth distance at higher latitude (because the scale is expanded): Earth distance ∝ cos latitude. Example: 10 cm represents 100 NM at 30° N → at 60° N it represents 100 × cos 60 / cos 30 = 57.7 NM.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Measure distances on a Mercator chart with the latitude scale at the mid-latitude of the line.

los.lo: State the properties of a Lambert projection.
los.title: Lambert conformal conic properties
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Cone that cuts the Earth along two standard parallels; conformal.
  • Meridians are straight lines converging towards the apex (pole); parallels are arcs of concentric circles.
  • Chart convergency = d.long × sin (parallel of origin), constant across the chart; correct at the parallel of origin.
  • Straight line ≈ great circle (good enough for navigation).
  • Scale correct on the standard parallels, slightly contracted between them (minimum at the parallel of origin), expanded outside them.
  • Rhumb lines are curves concave to the pole.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Standard ICAO chart at mid-latitudes (Jeppesen en-route charts, ICAO 1:500 000).
  • Parallel of origin lies between the standard parallels (approximately in the middle).

los.lo: Calculate straight line track changes on a Lambert chart.
los.title: Straight-line track changes on a Lambert chart
los.html:
Theory & physics

The true track of a straight line changes by the chart convergency = d.long × n. Example: n = 0.75, straight line from 010° W (initial track 060° T) to 020° E (d.long 30°): change = 22.5° → final track 082.5° T (NH eastbound, increasing).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Track change depends on d.long and n only, not on the latitudes of the points.

los.lo: Explain the scale variation throughout the charts as follows: the scale indicated on the chart will be correct at the standard parallels; the scale will increase away from the parallel of origin; the scale within the standard parallels differs by less than 1 per cent from the scale stated on the chart.
los.title: Lambert scale variation
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Scale is exactly as stated on the two standard parallels.
  • Between them the scale is slightly smaller (contracted), smallest at the parallel of origin.
  • Outside them the scale increases with distance from the parallel of origin.
  • If the standard parallels are separated by no more than about 2/3 of the chart's latitude range, the scale inside them differs from the stated scale by less than 1 %.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • "Constant scale" Lambert: treat the scale as constant for practical navigation.

los.lo: Given appropriate data, calculate initial, final or rhumb-line tracks between two positions (lat./long.).
los.title: Initial, final and rhumb-line tracks
los.html:
Theory & physics

Between two positions: RL track = average of initial and final GC tracks; initial GC = RL ∓ CA, final GC = RL ± CA, CA = ½ × d.long × sin mean lat. In the NH, eastbound, initial GC track < RL track < final GC track; westbound the opposite (tracks decreasing).

Example: initial GC track 050° T, final GC track 070° T → RL track 060° T, convergency 20°, CA 10°.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Sketch the meridians and the curve before answering: it removes sign errors.

los.lo: Given two positions (lat./long.) and information to determine convergency between the two positions, calculate the parallel of origin.
los.title: Finding the parallel of origin from convergency
los.html:
Theory & physics

If the change of track of a straight line (chart convergency) and the d.long are known: n = chart convergency / d.long, then parallel of origin = arcsin n. Example: straight-line track changes 18° over 24° of d.long → n = 0.75 → parallel of origin ≈ 48.6°.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Use chart convergency (straight-line track change), not Earth convergency.

los.lo: Given a Lambert chart, determine the parallel of origin, or constant of cone.
los.title: Determining parallel of origin or constant of the cone from a chart
los.html:
Theory & physics

Measure the angle between two meridians on the chart (chart convergency) and divide by their d.long: n = angle / d.long; parallel of origin = arcsin n. Alternatively, the chart legend states the standard parallels; the parallel of origin is approximately midway between them.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Example: meridians 10° apart meet at an angle of 7.5° → n = 0.75 → parallel of origin ≈ 48.6°.

los.lo: Given constant of cone or parallel of origin, great-circle track at one position and great-circle track at another position, calculate the difference of longitude between the two positions.
los.title: d.long from track change and constant of the cone
los.html:
Theory & physics

d.long = (final track − initial track) / n. Example: straight line on a Lambert chart with n = 0.6; track at A 075° T, at B 093° T → change 18° → d.long = 30° (B east of A in the NH, since track increased).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Direction: NH, track increasing → moving east.

los.lo: Recognise ICAO Annex 4 symbology.
los.title: ICAO Annex 4 symbology
los.html:
Theory & physics

Recognise the standard symbols: VOR (hexagon/compass rose), DME (square), VOR/DME (hexagon inside a square), VORTAC, NDB (dotted circle), aerodromes (civil, military, joint, with or without hard runways), obstacles (single, group, lit), airspace boundaries (controlled airspace, restricted (R), danger (D) and prohibited (P) areas), reporting points (compulsory: filled triangle; on request: open triangle), spot heights, MEF (maximum elevation figures).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Filled triangle = compulsory reporting point; open = on request.
  • P areas are prohibited; R restricted under conditions; D danger (activity may be hazardous).

los.lo: Measure tracks and distances on VFR and IFR en-route charts.
los.title: Measuring tracks and distances
los.html:
Theory & physics

Measure the track at the mid-meridian (Lambert) with a protractor aligned to a meridian; measure distance with dividers against the latitude scale near the mid-latitude, or with the chart's scale line. Convert true track to magnetic with the variation at mid-track (or use the magnetic tracks printed on IFR en-route charts).

Exam traps & operational impact

  • IFR en-route charts print magnetic tracks and distances on airways; VFR charts usually require you to measure true tracks.

los.lo: Fix the aircraft position on an en-route chart with information from VOR and DME equipment.
los.title: Fixing with VOR and DME
los.html:
Theory & physics

A VOR radial is a magnetic bearing from the station: convert to true with the variation at the station and draw it from the station. A DME range gives an arc around the station (slant range; for plotting ignore unless close to the station at height). Radial + DME from the same station gives a rho-theta fix; two radials or two DME ranges also fix.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • VOR: use station variation. NDB: use aircraft variation (the bearing is measured at the aircraft).
  • Close to a DME station at altitude, slant range is noticeably more than ground range.

los.lo: Resolve bearings of an NDB station for plotting on an aeronautical chart.
los.title: Plotting NDB bearings
los.html:
Theory & physics

The ADF measures a relative bearing (RB) at the aircraft. QDM (magnetic bearing to the station) = MH + RB. Convert to true with the variation at the aircraft: true bearing to the station (QUJ) = TH + RB. The bearing from the station (QTE) = QUJ ± 180°, and on a Lambert chart apply chart convergency between the aircraft's and the station's meridians before plotting from the station.

Example: TH 040°, RB 300° → QUJ = 340° T (at the aircraft) → QTE = 160° T measured at the aircraft's meridian; apply convergency to plot at the station's meridian.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • MH + RB = QDM; TH + RB = true bearing to the station.
  • Use variation at the aircraft for NDB bearings.
  • Ignore convergency only when both meridians are the same or the chart is Mercator (then use the conversion angle).

los.lo: Explain the concepts of a mean solar day and LMT.
los.title: Mean solar day and LMT
los.html:
Theory & physics

The apparent solar day (noon to noon) varies in length during the year because the orbit is elliptical and the axis tilted. The mean solar day is the average: exactly 24 h, based on a fictitious mean Sun moving uniformly. Local mean time (LMT) is time based on the mean Sun at a given meridian: 12:00 LMT when the mean Sun crosses the local meridian. Every meridian has its own LMT.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Sidereal day (relative to stars) ≈ 23 h 56 min; mean solar day = 24 h.
  • LMT at Greenwich = UTC (practically).

topics.title: Local Mean Time (LMT) and Universal Time Coordinated (UTC)

los.lo: Perform LMT and UTC calculations.
los.title: LMT and UTC conversions
los.html:
Theory & physics

The Earth turns 360° in 24 h: 15° = 1 h, 1° = 4 min, 15' = 1 min. Convert longitude into time (arc to time): LMT = UTC + longitude east; LMT = UTC − longitude west ("longitude east, Greenwich least; longitude west, Greenwich best").

Example: 0800 UTC at 045° E → LMT = 0800 + 3 h = 1100. At 082° 30' W → 5 h 30 min → LMT = 0230.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • 82°30' W: 82° = 5 h 28 min, 30' = 2 min → 5 h 30 min.
  • Crossing midnight changes the date: carry the day carefully.

topics.title: Standard time and daylight saving time

los.lo: Explain and apply the concept of standard time and daylight saving time, and perform standard time and daylight saving time calculations.
los.title: Standard time and daylight saving time
los.html:
Theory & physics

Standard time is the legal time used throughout a country or zone, usually a whole (sometimes half) number of hours from UTC. Daylight saving time (summer time) adds (usually) one hour to standard time during summer. Values for each country are listed in the AIP (GEN 2.1) and in almanacs; standard time is not a fixed function of longitude.

Example: Spain (mainland) standard time = UTC + 1; summer = UTC + 2.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Flight plans, METARs, NOTAMs use UTC; local time only for opening hours, often stated with "(summer)".
  • Convert local → UTC → other local; don't jump directly between local times.

los.lo: State the changes when crossing the International Date Line.
los.title: International Date Line
los.html:
Theory & physics

The International Date Line runs approximately along the 180° meridian, deviating around islands and countries. Crossing it westbound (from America towards Asia), add one day (the date advances). Crossing it eastbound (from Asia towards America), subtract one day. UTC itself never changes when crossing the date line; only local date changes.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Westbound: date + 1; eastbound: date − 1.
  • Work all timing problems in UTC to avoid date-line errors.

los.lo: Define sunrise, sunset, and civil twilight, and extract times from a suitable source (e.g. an almanac).
los.title: Sunrise, sunset and civil twilight
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Sunrise / sunset: when the upper edge (limb) of the Sun is on the visible horizon. Geometrically the Sun's centre is then about 50' below the horizon (16' semi-diameter + 34' refraction).
  • Civil twilight: the period between sunset and the moment the Sun's centre is 6° below the horizon (and the same in the morning before sunrise). Night (for aviation) is often defined using the end of evening civil twilight to the beginning of morning civil twilight.
  • Times are tabulated in LMT in the almanac for the latitude and date; convert to UTC with longitude.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Tables give LMT: convert with arc-to-time to get UTC, then to standard time.
  • Nautical twilight (12°) and astronomical (18°) are not used for aviation night.

los.lo: Explain the changes to sunrise, sunset, and civil twilight times with date, latitude and altitude.
los.title: How sunrise, sunset and twilight change
los.html:
Theory & physics

  • Date: days lengthen in spring and summer, shorten in autumn and winter.
  • Latitude: at the equator sunrise/sunset ≈ 0600/1800 LMT all year and twilight is short (Sun sets steeply). At higher latitudes daylight varies more and twilight lasts longer (the Sun sets at a shallow angle); in high-latitude summer, twilight can last all night.
  • Altitude: from height you see further over the horizon: sunrise is earlier and sunset later than on the ground.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Twilight is longest at high latitudes in summer, shortest at the equator.
  • At altitude after ground sunset, the aircraft may still be in sunlight while the ground is dark.

los.lo: Explain at which time of the year the duration of daylight changes at the highest rate.
los.title: When daylight changes fastest
los.html:
Theory & physics

The duration of daylight changes fastest around the equinoxes (March and September), when the Sun's declination changes most rapidly, and slowest around the solstices (June and December), when the declination is near its maximum and almost stationary.

Exam traps & operational impact

  • Equinox → fastest change; solstice → day length almost constant for a few weeks.
